strengths: Compelling and important motivation: evaluating set-valued hypothesis generation under underdetermination addresses a fundamental blind spot in standard single-answer benchmark evaluations for LLM-assisted scientific discovery.

Rigorous, non-circular evaluation methodology: because the admissible hypothesis space $H_O$ is explicitly enumerated and checked with deterministic validators and canonicalizers, Validity, Uniqueness, and Recovery can be measured objectively without relying on subjective LLM-as-judge evaluations.

Insightful theoretical and empirical characterization of mode collapse: the paper clearly formalizes why peaked generators exhibit a high-validity, low-recovery failure mode and demonstrates empirically that even state-of-the-art reasoning models suffer from severe simplicity bias and coverage collapse as the hypothesis space grows.

Comprehensive experimental suite: evaluation spans seven frontier models (both reasoning and non-reasoning) across three synthetic domains as well as a real-world biological case study (yeast vesicle-trafficking data), supplemented by detailed error breakdowns and information-theoretic exploration analyses.
weaknesses: Dependency on ground-truth complexity distribution in stratified decoding: the proposed complexity-stratified decoding allocates queries proportionally to the ground-truth distribution of complexities, which limits its applicability to real-world open-ended discovery where the underlying distribution over complexity levels is unknown a priori.

Limited coverage curves across variable sampling budgets: the primary experiments fix the sampling budget to $N = |H_O|$; reporting Recovery Rate as a continuous function of $N$ in the main text across tasks would give a more complete picture of asymptotic coverage and sample efficiency.

Stylized and discrete problem domains: while intentional as a diagnostic benchmark, the tasks are restricted to relatively small, discrete combinatorial structures (small DAGs, Boolean formulas, low-resolution voxel grids), leaving open how well these insights translate to scientific problems involving continuous parameters or unconstrained hypotheses.

Missing instance counts in the main text: while means and standard deviations are reported across instances in Tables 1–3, the exact dataset size (number of problem instances per task and difficulty level) is not prominently detailed in the main text.

strengths: Conceptual formulation: Formulating scientific hypothesis generation as set-valued inference under underdetermination provides an important conceptual shift from traditional single-answer correctness benchmarks to distributional coverage.

Deterministic and objective evaluation: By explicitly enumerating the finite admissible hypothesis space $H_O$ and using algorithmic validators and task-specific canonicalizers, the benchmark avoids the circularity, variance, and subjectivity of LLM-as-a-judge approaches.

Comprehensive empirical investigation: Evaluates a wide selection of state-of-the-art reasoning and non-reasoning models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, DeepSeek-R1, Grok-4, GPT-4o, LLaMA-3.3-70B), convincingly demonstrating that high validity frequently masks severe mode collapse and simplicity bias.

Concrete mitigation strategy: Proposes complexity-stratified decoding as a practical, training-free intervention that demonstrably improves exploration in under-represented, higher-complexity hypothesis subspaces.
Grounded real-world validation: Complements synthetic combinatorial tasks with a well-motivated biological case study on yeast double-knockout viability data.
weaknesses: Oracle dependency in stratified decoding: As noted in Section 6, the query budget across complexity levels is allocated proportionally to the ground-truth distribution of $H_O$. In actual underdetermined scientific problems where $H_O$ is unknown, this allocation distribution is unavailable, limiting the plug-and-play practicality of the mitigation.

Modest problem scale: Due to the requirement of exhaustive ground-truth enumeration, the experimental domains operate on modest scales (e.g., 4–6 node causal DAGs, $3\times 3\times 3$ voxel grids), which may constrain how findings generalize to open-ended or high-dimensional scientific search spaces.

Theoretical novelty is incremental: Section 4 provides a clear and useful intuitive explanation via a head-tail coupon-collector-style bound, but framing this standard probabilistic property as a core theoretical contribution slightly overstates its novelty.

Clarification needed on prompting and history: In Section 3, proposals are described as independent samples $P = \{\tilde{h}_1, \dots, \tilde{h}_N\}$, but in Section 5 the generation function includes an accumulator history $A$ ($F_{\text{LLM}}(O, A, T_{\text{prompt}})$). The paper should more clearly delineate the differences between parallel i.i.d. sampling versus sequential in-context reject-and-sample protocols in the main text.

strengths: Compelling and timely problem formulation: Moving beyond single-answer accuracy to set-valued inference under underdetermination addresses a critical blind spot in evaluating LLMs for scientific reasoning and exploration.

Rigorous, non-subjective evaluation framework: By focusing on domains where the admissible hypothesis set $H_O$ can be exhaustively enumerated, the benchmark eliminates LLM-as-judge circularity and evaluator subjectivity, providing exact calculations for Validity (VR), Uniqueness (NR), and Recovery (RR).

Clean theoretical grounding: Section 4 provides an intuitive and mathematically sound explanation (via head-tail distribution decomposition) formalizing why high validity naturally coexists with poor coverage (mode collapse) under peaked generators.

Extensive empirical evaluation and diagnostics: The paper evaluates a comprehensive suite of frontier reasoning and instruction-tuned models across diverse tasks, enriched by insightful ablation analyses (e.g., simplicity bias, information-theoretic entropy growth, and failure mode decomposition).

Constructive mitigation strategy: The introduction of complexity-stratified decoding offers an actionable, training-free approach that demonstrably unlocks previously undiscovered complex hypotheses across multiple models.
weaknesses: Stylized and combinatorial task domains: The three core tasks (causal DAGs, 3D voxel stacks, and Boolean formulas) are discrete combinatorial abstractions rather than rich, continuous, or noisy real-world scientific problems. While Section 8 introduces a yeast genetic interaction case study, it is limited to a single small instance.

Scalability constraints of exact enumeration: The core requirement of exact enumeration necessarily caps the problem sizes (e.g., up to 6 nodes for causal graphs or $3\times 3\times 3$ grids for voxels), leaving open the question of how to diagnose set-valued inference in large-scale spaces where $|H_O|$ is computationally intractable to enumerate.

Evaluation focused primarily on independent i.i.d. sampling: The baseline protocol evaluates independent draws with $N = |H_O|$. While natural for testing intrinsic model distributions, practical scientific exploration often leverages iterative, history-aware prompting (e.g., sequential dialogue with duplicate rejection or feedback), which is only partially explored in the main paper.

Mixed performance of complexity-stratified decoding: While stratified decoding improves complex hypothesis discovery, Table 4 shows notable degradations in overall recovery rate for several top-performing models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 dropping from 25.6% to 6.4%, and GPT-5 dropping by 7.7%), warranting a clearer characterization of when this intervention is advantageous.

strengths: Sound conceptual framing: Framing hypothesis generation under scientific underdetermination as set-valued inference is insightful and addresses a significant blind spot in current LLM benchmarks that reward only single-shot point predictions.

Objective, non-LLM evaluation: Grounding the evaluation in three combinatorial domains with deterministic forward validators and semantic canonicalization eliminates rater subjectivity and the circularity of LLM-as-judge.

Principled metrics grounded in creativity literature: Decomposing set-valued generation into Validity (appropriateness), Novelty/Uniqueness (originality), and Recovery (coverage/fluency) provides clear diagnostic axes.

Information-theoretic analysis: The cumulative entropy and information-gain analyses (Figures 3 and 4) offer an intuitive and mechanistic view into how models experience premature saturation and exploration decay.
weaknesses: Critical ambiguity in the sampling protocol: Section 3 states that models are evaluated by drawing 'N independent samples P = {h_1, ..., h_N}', whereas the formal task definitions in Section 4 (Eqs. 4.1–4.3) include an explicit history parameter A_h in F_LLM(..., A_h, ...). Furthermore, the conclusion suggests 'explicit memory across samples' as a future direction. It is unclear whether models were queried sequentially with previously generated hypotheses in-context, sampled independently via i.i.d. queries, or prompted to output a set all at once.

Missing theoretical baseline for i.i.d. sampling: If samples are drawn independently with replacement and budget N = |H_O|, the expected coverage under uniform random sampling over H_O is 1 - (1 - 1/|H_O|)^{|H_O|} approx 1 - 1/e approx 63.2% due to the coupon-collector effect. Without establishing this baseline, it is difficult to untangle genuine algorithmic mode collapse from the mathematical expectation of independent sampling.

Missing benchmark and experimental details: The manuscript does not report the number of problem instances evaluated per difficulty level, nor the exact values or ranges of |H_O| (except for a passing mention of |H_O|=27 for 3D task 3). Additionally, Appendix C refers readers to an external repository for prompts and hyperparameters, but no prompts or decoding parameters (e.g., temperature, top-p) are provided in the paper itself, impairing reproducibility.

Task realism vs. claims of scientific discovery: While the authors acknowledge that HypoSpace abstracts core ingredients rather than real-world discovery, the tasks (small DAG enumeration, voxel stacking under gravity, and depth-bounded Boolean formulas) are essentially synthetic combinatorial puzzles. The paper would benefit from a more cautious discussion regarding how well these findings transfer to semi-structured or natural-language scientific hypothesis spaces.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Framing LLM scientific reasoning and creativity as set-valued hypothesis generation under underdetermination addresses an important gap in traditional single-answer correctness benchmarks.

Principled metrics grounded in creativity theory: The decomposition into Validity (appropriateness), Uniqueness (originality), and Recovery (fluency/coverage) provides an intuitive, structured framework for evaluating solution space coverage.

Objective, non-LLM ground-truth evaluation: The use of formally verifiable domains (causal DAGs, 3D voxel stacking under gravity, Boolean logic) enables deterministic validation and exact coverage calculation, avoiding the circularity and subjectivity of LLM-as-a-judge approaches.
weaknesses: Critical contradictions in the sampling protocol: Section 3 states that models are evaluated by drawing '$N$ independent samples ... from a fixed prompt and decoding setup', whereas Section 4 defines generation as conditioned on prior history $A_{\tilde{G}}$ (i.e., sequential generation: $F_{LLM}(O, A_{\tilde{G}}, T_{prompt})$). It is fundamentally unclear whether samples were drawn independently (i.i.d.) or autoregressively with past attempts in context.

Statistically implausible results under the claimed protocol: In Table 1, multiple models achieve exactly 100.00% ± 0.00% on VR, NR, and RR simultaneously when sampling budget $N = |H_O|$. If samples are drawn independently, obtaining 100% unique valid coverage with $N = |H_O|$ draws without replacement/collisions is statistically impossible under standard probabilistic decoding. If generation was sequential with history, this contradicts the stated independent sampling protocol.

Missing vital experimental and decoding parameters: Mode collapse and diversity in LLMs are heavily governed by decoding parameters (e.g., temperature, top-$p$, presence/absence of seed/history). The manuscript omits all temperature and sampling hyperparameters, provides no prompt templates, and fails to state the number of problem instances evaluated per task and difficulty level (Appendix C merely states 'provided in our repository', but no repository or link is provided).

Dubious and unverifiable model evaluations: The evaluation reports results on unreleased or fictitious models with purported release dates in mid/late 2025 (e.g., 'GPT-5 released August 7, 2025', 'Gemini-2.5-Pro', 'Claude-Opus-4', 'Grok-4'), along with implausible pricing in Table 2 (e.g., Claude Opus at $1.00/1M tokens). This casts severe doubt on the validity and reproducibility of the reported empirical findings.

Under-specified task formalisms: In the Boolean interaction task, the set of syntactic trees representing a truth table is combinatorially explosive or infinite without rigid depth and grammar constraints; the exact bounding, canonicalization rules, and enumeration procedure for $H_O$ are insufficiently specified to permit verification.

strengths: Relevant and well-motivated conceptual framing: Viewing LLM hypothesis generation under underdetermination as set-valued inference and evaluating coverage (Recovery), non-redundancy (Uniqueness), and Validity addresses a key blind spot of single-answer accuracy benchmarks.

Objective, deterministic validation: Grounding the evaluation in three formal domains (causal DAGs under interventions, 3D voxel reconstruction under gravity constraints, and Boolean genetic expressions) eliminates LLM-as-a-judge subjectivity and circularity.

Interesting empirical focus on mode collapse: Examining whether models can systematically explore the full space of admissible solutions rather than repeatedly proposing familiar templates is an important direction for scientific reasoning.
weaknesses: Fundamental contradiction in the sampling protocol: Section 3 explicitly defines the protocol as drawing 'N independent samples P = {h_1, ..., h_N}', but Section 4 specifies generation conditioned on prior history A_h (e.g., F_LLM(O, A_G, T_prompt)). If sampling is independent, achieving 100% Uniqueness (NR) and 100% Recovery (RR) with budget N = |H_O| is statistically impossible due to the birthday/coupon-collector phenomenon (expected coverage for uniform independent sampling is ~63.2%). If sampling is sequential with memory in-context, it is not independent sampling, and this contradiction undermines the clarity and rigor of the experimental methodology.

Flawed coverage evaluation budget (N = |H_O|): Setting the sampling budget strictly to N = |H_O| conflates hypothesis recovery with zero-redundancy precision. For any stochastic sampler, assessing coverage typically requires evaluating Recovery as a function of sample count (e.g., RR@k for k > |H_O|) to disentangle entropy/exploration from strict single-pass permutation sampling.

Severe lack of experimental details and reproducibility: The manuscript never reports the number of problem instances evaluated per task, the distribution of |H_O| across tasks (apart from a single passing mention of |H_O|=27), or the evaluation prompts and generation hyperparameters (temperature, top_p, etc.). Appendix C defers full prompts and settings to 'our repository', but no link or text is provided anywhere in the paper.

Disjoint theoretical formulation in Section 3.2: The Bayesian formulation of divergent creativity (defining posterior plausibility P(h_i | O), thresholded count C_count, and Shannon entropy C_entropy) is entirely disconnected from the actual experiments, as the paper admits models cannot estimate these posterior distributions and instead defines empirical pattern frequencies in Section 3.3.

Unverifiable model evaluations and provenance issues: The empirical evaluation benchmarks unreleased or fictional models and snapshots (e.g., GPT-5 dated August 2025, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Grok-4), making the empirical findings ungrounded and impossible to verify or replicate.
